title: Le e muet
intro: French has a little **e** that often disappears: the **e muet**. It's written **e**, with no accent, and when you hear it, it sounds /ə/. Knowing when it drops makes your French sound natural, and helps you understand people who speak fast: *samedi* is /sam.di/, and *je ne sais pas* often sounds like /ʃɛ pa/.

cases.label: the final e is silent
cases.rule: A plain **e** at the end of a word is silent: *une table* /tabl/, *la porte* /pɔʁt/, *il parle* /paʁl/. But it makes you **say the consonant before it**: *petit* /pə.ti/ → *petite* /pə.tit/, *grand* /ɡʁɑ̃/ → *grande* /ɡʁɑ̃d/.

cases.label: dropped inside a word: samedi
cases.rule: Inside a word, an **e** between two single consonants usually drops: *samedi* /sam.di/, *maintenant* /mɛ̃t.nɑ̃/, *acheter* /aʃ.te/, *boulangerie* /bu.lɑ̃ʒ.ʁi/, *lentement* /lɑ̃t.mɑ̃/.

cases.label: kept to avoid three consonants: vendredi
cases.rule: If dropping the **e** would put **three consonants** together, you keep it: *vendredi* /vɑ̃.dʁə.di/, *mercredi* /mɛʁ.kʁə.di/, *appartement* /a.paʁ.tə.mɑ̃/, *je parlerai* /paʁ.lə.ʁe/.

cases.label: kept at the start: demain, devant
cases.rule: In the first syllable of a word, careful speech keeps the **e**: *demain* /də.mɛ̃/, *devant* /də.vɑ̃/, *fenêtre* /fə.nɛtʁ/. In fast speech, after a vowel, it often drops: *à demain* → /a dmɛ̃/.

cases.label: small words: je, ne, de, le…
cases.rule: The small words **je, me, te, se, le, de, ne, que, ce** all have this **e**. In everyday speech, many lose it: *je ne sais pas* → /ʒən sɛ pa/ or /ʃɛ pa/; *pas de problème* → /pad pʁɔ.blɛm/. When several come together, drop one **e** in two: *je te le dis* → /ʒət lə di/.

cases.label: -ent: silent in verbs, /ɑ̃/ elsewhere
cases.rule: The verb ending **-ent** (ils, elles) is silent: *ils parlent* sounds exactly like *il parle*. In other words, **-ent** is /ɑ̃/: *le vent, souvent, lentement, un parent*.

cases.label: é, è, ê are never silent
cases.rule: Only a plain **e** can disappear. With an accent, you always say it: *été* /e.te/, *père* /pɛʁ/, *fête* /fɛt/.

sections.title: 1. The final e

examples.en: A little boy and a little girl.

sections.tip: That's why the feminine often *sounds* different: you hear the consonant before the silent **e**: *petit / petite, grand / grande, vert / verte*.

examples.en: On Saturday, I'm going to the bakery.

sections.title: 3. Three consonants: keep the e
text: Say *samedi* /sam.di/, but *vendredi* /vɑ̃.dʁə.di/: without its **e**, *vendredi* would put **d-r-d** together.

examples.en: I work on Wednesday and Friday.

sections.title: 4. At the start of a word
text: In careful speech, like the voice in this app, the **e** of a first syllable stays: *demain, devant*. In fast conversation, after a vowel, you'll often hear it drop.

examples.en: The bus is in front of the station.

sections.title: 5. Small words: je, ne, de, le…
text: In everyday speech, the **e** of *je, me, te, se, le, de, ne, que, ce* often disappears. With two or three small words in a row, drop one **e** in two.
sections.tip: The voice in this app speaks carefully and keeps these **e**'s. Real conversations are faster: listen for *j'sais pas* in films and songs!

mistakes.why: The **e** between **m** and **d** drops: two syllables.
Keep the **e**: without it, three consonants would meet.

story.title: Tom à la boulangerie
story.en: Saturday morning: Tom buys some bread… and discovers that French people swallow their e's.

lines.fr: {Samedi|e-middle} matin, Tom va à la {boulangerie|e-middle}, en bas de chez lui.
lines.en: Saturday morning: Tom goes to the bakery downstairs from his flat.

lines.fr: Il veut {acheter|e-middle} du pain et deux croissants.
lines.en: He wants to buy some bread and two croissants.

lines.fr: Bonjour, monsieur ! Qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?
lines.en: Good morning! What can I get you?

lines.fr: Une baguette et deux croissants, s'il vous plaît.
lines.en: A baguette and two croissants, please.

lines.fr: Ah, désolée, il n'y a plus de croissants. Revenez {demain|e-start} !
lines.en: Oh, sorry, there are no croissants left. Come back tomorrow!

lines.fr: {Je ne sais pas|e-small} si je peux venir {demain|e-start}…
lines.en: I don't know if I can come tomorrow…

lines.fr: {Pas de problème|e-small} ! Je vous les garde.
lines.en: No problem! I'll keep them for you.

lines.fr: La boulangère parle vite. Tom n'entend pas tous les e : « je ne sais pas » devient presque « j'sais pas » !
lines.en: The baker talks fast. Tom doesn't hear all the e's: 'je ne sais pas' almost becomes 'j'sais pas'!
In the street, Tom softly repeats: 'maintenant, samedi, lentement'.

lines.fr: Mais dans « {mercredi|e-three} » et « {vendredi|e-three} », il garde le e : sans lui, il y aurait trois consonnes ensemble.
lines.en: But in 'mercredi' and 'vendredi', he keeps the e: without it, there would be three consonants together.

lines.fr: Devant son {appartement|e-three}, il rencontre ses voisines. {Elles parlent|e-ent} anglais avec lui : elles veulent apprendre !
lines.en: Outside his flat, he meets his neighbours. They speak English with him: they want to learn!
No, no! I speak French now!

lines.fr: Il rentre chez lui et il appelle son {père|e-accent}, en Angleterre.
lines.en: He goes home and calls his father, in England.

lines.fr: Papa, j'ai {été|e-accent} à la boulangerie… et j'ai parlé comme un vrai Français !
lines.en: Dad, I've been to the bakery… and I talked like a real French person!

lines.fr: Il y a du {vent|e-ent}, la {fenêtre|e-start} est ouverte, et Tom mange sa baguette. Une {petite|e-final} victoire !
lines.en: It's windy, the window's open, and Tom eats his baguette. A little victory!
